screens.title: Final Examination and Answer Key
screens.subtitle: A guided review of the exam structure, model answers, and common pitfalls to prepare you for real ROS development.

narration.text: This final chapter is your guided review. It walks through the exam structure, explains why each question matters, and shows the correct answers with practical reasoning. You will review multiple-choice items that test core concepts like topics, services, and actions; short-answer prompts that require explanation and examples; code-analysis questions that reveal common runtime bugs; and a practical design problem that ties components into a working system. Each section includes the correct answers and the reasoning behind them. As you study, pay attention to why certain answers are correct and what common confusions lead to mistakes. For example, many learners mix up the registry role of the ROS Master with message forwarding, or forget to keep Python nodes alive with the appropriate loop. By the end of this chapter you will not only know the right answers but also understand the practical implications for writing and debugging ROS systems. Take a moment to ask yourself which topics you want to revisit after this review.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll master by studying this exam and answer key

narration.text: These objectives make the exam review actionable. You will identify the correct ROS communication primitive for different tasks and explain why topics, services, and actions are distinct. You will diagnose runtime bugs in Python and C++ nodes and prescribe fixes like adding a spin loop or checking for preemption. You will configure systems with launch files and parameters so nodes can reuse the same code in simulation and hardware. Finally, you will design a multi-node system that meets functional requirements, handles preemption, and uses the parameter server correctly. Each objective pairs conceptual clarity with a concrete skill: choosing topics for streaming sensor data, writing services for discrete requests, using actions when feedback and cancellation matter, and reading launch files to fix remapping and parameter scope mistakes. By the end, you should be able to argue why a given answer is correct, not just select it. This helps in interviews, debugging sessions, and real robot deployments.

screens.title: Core definitions and exam reasoning
screens.subtitle: Why certain choices are correct and what they test

narration.text: Multiple-choice questions in Section A test precise definitions and common usage. For example, the question "What is ROS?" checks whether you understand ROS as middleware — a communication infrastructure that connects nodes — rather than a real-time OS, a language, or hardware. The correct choice is the middleware definition because ROS provides topics, services, actions, and a parameter server to enable distributed robot components to exchange messages. Another question asks the role of the ROS Master. Many learners mistakenly imagine it forwards messages; in fact it is a central registry that connects publishers and subscribers by name. This matters because if you incorrectly assume the Master forwards messages you may look for forwarding settings instead of checking name resolution and namespace issues. A further test asks which mechanism is best for streaming sensor data; the exam expects topics since they are one-way, asynchronous streams. A quick study tip: read each option and map it back to the communication characteristic being tested — synchronous vs asynchronous, streaming vs request-response, or feedback and cancellation. By practicing this mapping you will answer similar items reliably.

keyIdea.title: MCQ strategy
keyIdea.text: Map options to the communication characteristics: streaming, synchronous, or preemptible feedback.

content.html:
Section A Multiple Choice
Definitions
Key definitions the exam checks:
  • ROS — middleware framework providing communication infrastructure for robots.
  • ROS Master — central registry that matches publishers and subscribers by name.
  • Topic — asynchronous stream suitable for sensor data.
  • Service — synchronous request-response for discrete tasks.
  • Action — asynchronous, cancellable task with feedback and result.
Common misconception
Don't assume Master forwards messages. If connections fail, check name resolution and namespaces first.
Practice mapping
Given a scenario, pick the primitive by matching behavior:
Streaming camera frames
Use topics — continuous flow, many subscribers can listen.
Request battery level
Use a service — single request, immediate response.
Navigate to a waypoint with progress
Use an action — long running, needs feedback and cancellation.

screens.title: Topics vs Services & Parameter Server
screens.subtitle: Clear contrasts, practical examples, and configuration best practices

narration.text: Section B asks you to explain differences and give examples. Start with topics versus services: a topic is a one-way, asynchronous channel for streaming data. Publishers send messages continuously and do not wait for responses. Use topics for sensors like cameras or lidar where many nodes may subscribe. A service is synchronous and blocking: a client sends a request and waits for a response, so it suits discrete queries such as reading a battery level or toggling an LED. A concrete example from the answer key: a camera publishes on a topic named camera image raw to stream images, while get battery level is implemented as a service to return a single numeric value on demand. Next, the Parameter Server is a shared key-value store available while roscore runs. It separates configuration from code; you can load parameters from a YAML file to change PID gains or patrol intervals without changing source. This is essential when running the same nodes in simulation and on different robots. A common mistake is hardcoding values instead of using parameters. Before submitting an answer, always include a short example and show why the separation of code and config matters in deployment.

keyIdea.title: Why params matter
keyIdea.text: Parameters let you change behavior without recompiling; use YAML and launch files to manage environment differences.

content.html:
Section B Short Answer
Definition cards
Topic
Asynchronous, one-way stream. Example: /camera/image_raw for continuous images.
Service
Synchronous request-response. Example: /get_battery_level returns a single value on demand.
Parameter Server
Shared key-value store for runtime configuration, loaded at roscore startup or via launch files.
Process: choosing the right tool
Steps to decide:
  1. Is this continuous data or a single query? If continuous, use a topic.
  2. Does the caller need a blocking response? If yes, use a service.
  3. Does the operation take time and need feedback or cancellation? Use an action.
Example
A camera publishes images on a topic; a dashboard subscribes. A client queries battery level via a service when needed.

screens.title: Keep nodes alive: rospy.spin and structure
screens.subtitle: Diagnose the missing spin and best-practice structure for Python nodes

narration.text: The first code-analysis question shows a simple Python subscriber that never calls the function to keep the node alive. The node creates a subscriber and then the script exits, so callbacks never run. The missing call is the one that enters the ROS event loop; in rospy that is rospy. spin(). Add rospy. spin() after creating the subscriber so the process keeps running and processes callbacks. A good pattern also wraps node initialization in a guarded main block using if name == 'main': so the node can be imported safely in tests. Here is a concise fix: add a final line calling rospy. spin(), and wrap initialization in the main guard. A common misconception is to assume subscribers run as soon as they are created and that the script will stay alive; in native Python a script ends unless you block or sleep. Another subtle point: ensure the subscriber callback is lightweight or delegates heavy work to other threads, to avoid blocking message handling. Finally, always test the node by running roscore and using rostopic echo to confirm messages arrive and are printed by the listener. How will you test this fix on a real system?

keyIdea.title: Spin keeps callbacks active
keyIdea.text: Always call rospy.spin() or otherwise block the main thread so callbacks execute and the node remains registered.

content.html:
Section C Code Analysis
Original snippet
import rospy
from std_msgs.msg import String

def callback(msg):
    print(msg.data)

rospy.init_node('listener')
sub = rospy.Subscriber('/chatter', String, callback)
Problem: script exits immediately because there is no event loop to process callbacks.
Corrected pattern
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import rospy
from std_msgs.msg import String

def callback(msg):
  print(msg.data)

if __name__ == '__main__':
  rospy.init_node('listener')
  sub = rospy.Subscriber('/chatter', String, callback)
  rospy.spin()
Test with roscore and publishing to /chatter. Verify the listener prints messages and stays alive.

screens.title: Scope and placement of parameters in launch files
screens.subtitle: Fixing a misplaced param and ensuring executables are runnable

narration.text: The launch-file question shows a param tag placed outside of a node, which makes it global rather than private. If the intention is to set a private parameter for a node, put the param inside the node tag. For example, max speed intended for my node should be nested so it appears as a private parameter under that node's namespace. Another practical issue is executable permissions for Python node scripts. If the node is a Python file, it must have executable permission and a proper shebang line so rosrun and roslaunch can execute it directly. A second important launch concept is remapping. The remap tag redirects topic or service names to another name; use it when you want the same node to publish or subscribe under different names in different runs. Common mistakes include wrong nesting, missing executable bit, and forgetting to source the workspace setup file so new nodes and messages are visible. When you edit a launch file, test by running roslaunch and checking logs for parameter values and node names to confirm the intended scope. Scope and placement of parameters in launch files means place private parameters inside node tags and ensure python nodes are executable with a proper shebang.. In practical terms, fixing a misplaced param and ensuring executables are runnable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: rosbag recording and topic name exactness
screens.subtitle: Why exact topic names and queue_size matter for reliable data capture

narration.text: The exam asks which command records topic data for later playback. The correct command is rosbag record. Use rosbag to capture messages for debugging, replay, and dataset collection. While recording, exact topic names matter: a leading slash changes the fully-qualified name, so /robot_news and robot_news are different topics. When subscribers are not receiving messages, mismatched topic names are a common cause. Another relevant parameter is queue_size in a publisher. Queue size limits how many outgoing messages are buffered before old ones are dropped; for high-rate sensors you may want a larger queue to avoid drop but this increases memory usage. Conversely, a tiny queue can lead to dropped messages when subscribers are slow. Finally, when recording and replaying rosbags, verify the message types match between writer and reader; message type mismatches can prevent successful deserialization. In practice, test recording and playback with a short rosbag and confirm the dashboard subscriber sees the same messages when you replay them. This exercise helps ensure your logging and testing workflows are robust. rosbag recording and topic name exactness means use rosbag record to capture exact topic names; verify names and message types during replay.. screens.title: Actions: feedback, cancellation, and server responsibilities
screens.subtitle: Why action servers must check for preemption and manage loop rates

narration.text: The C++ action server example in the exam reveals two important runtime responsibilities. First, an action server must check for preemption requests. Clients can cancel goals and expect the server to stop work and set a preempted result. If the server ignores preemption and always sets success, clients receive incorrect outcomes. The exam provides a fix: inside the execution loop call isPreemptRequested and set preempted before returning. Second, long-running loops should include a sleep or rate control so they don't run at maximum C P U, which can starve other processes. The example also sends periodic feedback percent complete, which is how actions communicate progress to clients. A concrete scenario: a camera node performing a ten-second inspection should publish feedback each second and respond immediately if the patrol controller cancels the inspection. A common misconception is to treat actions like services; unlike services they are not blocking single-step calls but interactive tasks that can be canceled and report progress. When writing an action server, always test cancellation behavior with a client that sends and then cancels goals mid-execution. Actions: feedback, cancellation, and server responsibilities means action servers must check for cancellation, publish feedback, and respect client preemption to avoid false success reports.. In practical terms, why action servers must check for preemption and manage loop rates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Always handle preemption
keyIdea.text: Action servers must check for cancellation, publish feedback, and respect client preemption to avoid false success reports.

content.html:
Actions Preemption
Problematic pattern
for (int i = 0; i < goal->count; ++i) {
  my_pkg::MyActionFeedback feedback;
  feedback.percentage = float(i) / goal->count;
  _as.publishFeedback(feedback);
}
_as.setSucceeded(result);
Issue: no preemption checks and no rate limiting.
Robust fix
for (int i = 0; i < goal->count; ++i) {
  if (_as.isPreemptRequested()) {
    _as.setPreempted();
    return;
  }
  // publish feedback
  ros::Duration(0.1).sleep();
}
_as.setSucceeded(result);
Add preemption checks and a sleep to yield CPU and allow cancellations to take effect.

screens.title: Smart home patrol system architecture
screens.subtitle: Nodes, topics, services, actions, and parameters in the proposed design

narration.text: The practical problem asks you to design a smart home robot system that patrols and reports sensors. The supplied model answer defines clear responsibilities: sensor publisher for temperature, motion, and camera streams; patrol controller subscribing to motion and sending goals to an inspect action; camera node hosting the action server and publishing high-resolution images during inspection; alert service that logs alerts; and a dashboard that subscribes to display data. Parameters include house name, patrol interval, and alert threshold. This architecture separates streaming data from control logic. Temperature and camera images are topics because they are continuous or high-rate streams. Motion is a topic to quickly notify the patrol controller. The inspect operation is an action because it runs for a duration, provides feedback, and can be canceled. The alert mechanism is a service because sending an alert is a discrete request. The launch file starts all nodes and sets parameters so the same code runs in simulation or on hardware. This division of responsibilities reduces coupling and makes each node easier to test and reuse. Smart home patrol system architecture means use topics for streaming sensors, actions for long inspections, and services for discrete alerts to keep nodes focused and testable.. Design Architecture
Node responsibilities
sensor_publisher
Publishes /temperature (Float64), /motion (Bool), /camera/image_raw (Image) at configured rates.
patrol_controller
Subscribes to /motion. On detection, sends a goal to /inspect_area and calls /send_alert service.
camera_node
Hosts /inspect_area action server, publishes higher-res images during inspection, supports preemption.
alert_service
Provides /send_alert to log or forward alerts; discrete request-response service.
Parameters & launch
/house_name, /patrol_interval, /alert_threshold_temp set via launch file so behavior is configurable without code changes.

Design Implementation Notes
sensor_publisher snippet
# sensor_publisher.py
rospy.init_node('sensor_publisher')
temp_pub = rospy.Publisher('/temperature', Float64, queue_size=10)
motion_pub = rospy.Publisher('/motion', Bool, queue_size=10)
image_pub = rospy.Publisher('/camera/image_raw', Image, queue_size=10)
rate = rospy.Rate(1)
while not rospy.is_shutdown():
  # publish sensors
  rate.sleep()
Use queue_size and controlled rate so the publisher behaves well under load.
patrol_controller notes
Wait for the action server, send a goal, and handle the result or preemption. Call alert service with error handling for service exceptions.
Common cross-language causes
  • devel/setup.bash not sourced so new message packages not visible.
  • Message types not from the same package or differing definitions.
  • Topic name mismatches including leading slash differences.
  • Missing spin or spin-like loops so callbacks never run.

screens.title: Why subscribers fail and how to debug them
screens.subtitle: A checklist for the five frequent causes listed in the key answers

narration.text: The exam's answer list includes a troubleshooting question about a Python publisher and C++ subscriber that appear connected but do not communicate. The answer enumerates several possible causes which form a practical debugging checklist. First, ensure you have sourced devel/setup. bash so the C++ subscriber can find generated message types. Second, verify the message type names match exactly; different packages or definitions lead to incompatible serialized types. Third, check that topic names match exactly including leading slashes and namespaces. Fourth, confirm the subscriber is properly spinning or calling ros::spin/rospy. spin so callbacks are processed. Fifth, ensure the compiled executable is the one invoked by rosrun or launch file, and that permissions and names are correct. In practice, reproduce a minimal test: publish a simple message on the topic with rostopic pub and use rostopic echo to observe it. Use rqt_graph to view connections and confirm the publisher and subscriber appear linked. Addressing these five areas resolves the majority of cross-language communication issues. Why subscribers fail and how to debug them means source setup files, match message definitions, confirm exact topic names, ensure spin, and validate executable names.. In practical terms, a checklist for the five frequent causes listed in the key answers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Debug checklist
keyIdea.text: Source setup files, match message definitions, confirm exact topic names, ensure spin, and validate executable names.

content.html:
Debug Subscriber Failures
Five frequent causes
  1. Workspace not sourced: devel/setup.bash missing so messages not found.
  2. Message mismatch: types must be identical and generated from same package.
  3. Topic name mismatch: exact names and leading slashes matter.
  4. No spin: callbacks not processed without ros::spin or rospy.spin.
  5. Executable mismatch: wrong executable name in rosrun or launch file or permissions missing.
Diagnostic steps: use rostopic list/echo, rqt_graph, and rosbag to isolate where the pipeline breaks. Test with a minimal publisher or subscriber to confirm type and name alignment.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders from the answer key

narration.text: Here are three concise ideas to carry forward. First, map communication patterns to intent: topics for streaming, services for immediate queries, and actions for long-running tasks with feedback and cancellation. Second, configuration is crucial: use the Parameter Server and launch files to separate environment-specific settings from code and ensure parameters are scoped correctly. Third, debugging follows a simple checklist: verify message types and names, source the workspace, ensure nodes are spinning, and confirm executables and permissions. Keep these three concepts in mind when designing, debugging, or explaining ROS systems; they will resolve many common issues and let you scale confidently from examples to real robots.
